_readme: Golden-prompt corpus: real teacher asks and what the Create flow should
resolve each one to. Two consumers:
EXPECTED DELIVERABLE is deliverable today — the game validates, the
recipe compiles clean, the reference storyboard compiles from real
bricks. It does NOT call any AI.
2. scripts/eval-designer-prompts.js (manual, real AI): runs each prompt
through the live matcher and diffs what it chose against 'expect'.
Run it before AND after touching a matcher/storyboard prompt.
Kinds: host (a built-in game), recipe (id + params merged over defaults),
storyboard (a reference brick realization), cantBuild (documented honest
gap — the platform should say no, not fake it).

prompts.prompt: Students build sentences together, but each student adds only ONE word and cannot see any of the words written before theirs. At the end everyone sees the surprise sentence they started, finished by classmates.
Each student starts a story and passes it on. The next writer can only see the last few words of what came before, adds a line, and passes again. At the end the whole stories are revealed.
prompts.note: Nearest current match; a dedicated folded-story recipe on collect.showTail is the natural follow-on. story-builder is a defensible pick (same chain, no fold).

prompts.prompt: A fast-paced quiz with points for speed and a leaderboard at the end. I have my own multiple choice questions.
An icebreaker where each student writes two true statements and one lie about themselves and the class guesses which one is the lie.
Everyone answers one big question alone first, then pairs combine their answers into one stronger answer that the whole class sees.
A story that grows as it passes from student to student, each one adding to it, and at the end every story returns to the student who started it.
For review: students list what they remember from today's lesson from memory, then classmates add things the list missed, and it comes back to its author.
Students guess a number, like how many jelly beans are in the jar or how long the Amazon river is, and we see whose guess was closest.
Students draw a picture of a phrase, then everyone writes fake captions for each other's drawings and tries to spot the real one.
Each student writes a riddle about one of our vocabulary words, then the class sees each riddle and guesses the word.

storyboard.name: Vocab Riddles
storyboard.description: Write a riddle for a vocabulary word, then guess everyone else's.

steps.text: Pick one of our vocabulary words and keep it secret. You are going to write a riddle about it!
Your word and your riddle.
steps.clueLabel: Your riddle (no fair using the word!)

steps.text: Every word earned, every riddle solved. Nice work, wordsmiths.

prompts.note: KNOWN MISS 2026-08-30 baseline: the matcher picked recipe:creative-vote instead of handing off (noMatch) — it fakes a weak fit rather than letting the storyboard generator build the guessing-rounds shape. Matcher-prompt finding, parked.

prompts.prompt: Everyone rates their stress on a scale of 1 to 10, then predicts what the class average will be, and we see how close the predictions were.

storyboard.name: Guess the Class
storyboard.description: Rate yourself on a scale, then predict the class average.

steps.text: Two numbers coming up: first how YOU feel, then a prediction about the whole class.
On a scale of 1 to 10, how stressed are you feeling right now?
Now predict: what do you think the class average stress level will be, from 1 to 10?
That is the class, and that is how well you read it.

prompts.note: Owner built this on the live site 2026-09-12 and got a bare number box with no bounds; the estimate brick now carries min and max for a scale question, and the runtime reads the wording when it is missing (engine/phases/estimate-range.js).

prompts.prompt: Each student writes a hypothesis about tomorrow's egg drop experiment. It passes to a classmate who adds one piece of supporting evidence or reasoning, then to another classmate who adds a counterargument. At the end everyone sees what happened to the hypothesis they wrote.

storyboard.name: Hypothesis Relay
storyboard.description: A hypothesis travels: one classmate argues for it, another argues against, then it comes home.

steps.text: Science court is in session. You will write a hypothesis about tomorrow's egg drop, and two classmates will put it on trial.

steps.start: Write one hypothesis about tomorrow's egg drop experiment. What will happen, and to which design?
hops: Read the hypothesis above. Add ONE piece of supporting evidence or reasoning below it.
Read the hypothesis and the evidence above. Add ONE counterargument or complication below them.

steps.text: Every hypothesis got a defender and a skeptic. Tomorrow, the eggs decide.

prompts.note: The chain-brick case: per-hop instructions differ, so no fixed recipe covers it. idea-chain is a defensible near-match.

prompts.prompt: An activity where everyone shares what they're most afraid of and then you have to guess who shared what. And then afterwards you see everyone's answer and you collectively rank them in order of how scary you think they are.

storyboard.name: Fear Factor
storyboard.description: Share a fear, guess whose it is, then rank them together from scariest down.

steps.text: Everyone shares one thing they are afraid of. Then we find out how well we know each other: each fear goes up, and the class guesses whose it is.
What are you most afraid of? One honest line.
Every fear the class shared:
Put these in order, scariest at the top.
Brave room. Everyone is afraid of something, and now we know a little more about each other.

prompts.note: The prompt that found the dead storyboard door (2026-09-07). Needs guess:who on guessing-rounds (the typed-guess default guesses the secret) and the rank brick (a vote is not a ranking). Who Said It? covers the first half only.

prompts.prompt: writing prompt generator, the class everyone lists 4 people and 4 circumstances then they are shuffled and everyone gets one person and one circumstance.

storyboard.name: Prompt Generator
storyboard.description: Everyone adds a person and a circumstance, the piles are shuffled and dealt, and each student writes from the pair they drew.

steps.text: We are building writing prompts together. You will add a person and a circumstance to the piles. Then the piles get shuffled and you will be dealt one of each, invented by classmates, to write from.

piles.label: A person
piles.prompt: Name a person a story could be about. A lighthouse keeper, a substitute teacher on their first day, a retired spy who misses the work...

piles.label: A circumstance
piles.prompt: Name a circumstance, something happening or about to happen. Stuck in an elevator, the last day of summer, a power cut in the middle of an exam...

steps.text: Write the opening paragraph of a story that puts your person in your circumstance.
Every prompt in this room was built by three people. Keep yours, it is the start of something.

prompts.note: The shuffle-and-deal prompt (2026-09-07). Story Ingredients is the same mechanic with three fixed piles, a fine host answer; the deal brick lets the storyboard build it with the teacher's own piles.

prompts.prompt: I just want to ask the class one question and see everyone's answers on the board.

params.question: What is one thing you learned today?

prompts.prompt: Students record a two minute podcast segment about the chapter and we listen to them together.

expect.reason: No audio or video recording; the platform is text and simple taps.

prompts.prompt: My students are in teams. Each team picks a first and second choice among four categories (self and identity, working with others, thinking and problem solving, execution and adaptation). Each group decides on its top choices, and then the categories are assigned to the groups.
prompts.note: The owner's prompt (2026-09-16), which the storyboard could not build before the assign brick and the Choice Draft recipe existed.

prompts.prompt: Split the class into groups of three. Each group ranks the six chapter topics they would rather present, then give every group one topic so no more than two groups share a chapter. Finish by showing who got what.

storyboard.name: Chapter Draft
storyboard.description: Groups rank the chapters, then each is handed one.

steps.text: Time to divide up the chapters. Your group ranks the six chapters, favorite on top, and the draft hands each group one.
Which chapter would your group rather present? First choice at the top.
Here is who presents what.
Chapters are set. Start planning with your group.

prompts.note: The same shape with a teacher's own list and a cap per item: teams, rank as groups, assign (2026-09-16).

prompts.prompt: Debate pairs: partners get opposite sides of a question, write an opening argument, swap with their partner, write a rebuttal, then switch and argue the other side.

storyboard.name: Debate Pairs
storyboard.description: Partners argue opposite sides of one question, rebut each other, then switch.

steps.text: You and a partner will take opposite sides of one question. Argue yours, answer theirs, then trade places.
Should homework be banned? You are arguing {{side}}. Write your opening argument.
rounds: Read your partner's opening below. Write a rebuttal, still arguing {{side}}.
Switch sides: you now argue {{otherSide}}. Answer your partner's rebuttal below from that side.

steps.text: You argued both sides. Which one was harder to make?

prompts.note: The pairs-brick case (storyboard probe, 2026-09-20): the one idea a teacher got nothing for. Partners, rounds with the partner's piece in view, sides dealt and switched.

prompts.prompt: Watch this YouTube clip https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dQw4w9WgXcQ then answer two questions about it.

storyboard.name: Clip and Two Questions
storyboard.description: The class watches a clip on the projector, then answers two questions about it.

steps.text: Eyes up front. We are watching a short clip together, then you will answer two questions about it on your device.
In one sentence, what was the clip mostly about?
Here is what the class took from it:
What is one question the clip left you with?
The questions we still have:
Good watching. We will pick up those questions next time.

prompts.note: The video case (storyboard probe, 2026-09-20): the other idea a teacher got nothing for. The clip rides on the announce brick's video field and plays on the projector.

prompts.prompt: Groups of four, each member gets a job (Facilitator, Recorder, Timekeeper, Reporter), then the group works through a shared to-do list for the lab.

storyboard.name: Lab Jobs
storyboard.description: Groups of four, a job for every member, then one shared lab checklist per group.

steps.text: Lab day. You will be put in groups of four, every one of you gets a job, and your group works through today's list together.
Work through the lab with your group. Tagged tasks belong to a job, but everyone backs each other up.
tasks: Set up your station and check the materials
Timekeeper: call out the halfway point
Facilitator: make sure everyone has done a step
Clean up and return the materials

steps.text: Reporters, get ready to share what your group found.

prompts.note: The roles-brick case (storyboard probe, 2026-09-20): jobs per member had compiled to teams > rank > assign, which hands one job per GROUP. Group Work Day is the matcher's defensible answer.

prompts.prompt: Guess how many times the average heart beats in a day. Closest guess wins.

storyboard.name: Heartbeat Guess
storyboard.description: One number to estimate, the closest guess takes the points.

steps.text: One question, one number. Reason it out, lock in your guess, and the closest guess takes the points.
How many times does the average human heart beat in one day?
About a hundred thousand. Your heart did a few dozen of those while you guessed.

prompts.note: The estimate-answer case (storyboard probe, 2026-09-20): with an answer the estimate step reveals the number, the class spread, and closeness scores; without one it is a poll and no text may promise a winner. Estimation Station is the matcher's defensible answer.

prompts.prompt: Draw a monster, put all the drawings on the wall, and vote for the scariest one.

storyboard.name: Monster Wall
storyboard.description: Everyone draws a monster; after the teacher's look, the wall opens one drawing at a time, then the class votes for the scariest and the winner goes up under the crown.

steps.text: Ninety seconds to draw the scariest monster you can. Every drawing goes up on the wall, then you vote for the one that gives you chills.
Draw a monster. Scary, silly, or both, but make it yours.
steps.gallery: The monster wall is open. Look closely, you will be voting in a moment.

steps.text: That was the monster wall. Sleep well.

prompts.note: The draw-brick case (storyboard probe, 2026-09-20): declined 3 of 3 as typed-text-only while Draw Gallery did it. Since the vote over drawings (the same night) the ballot shows thumbnails and the crown shows the winning drawing. Draw Gallery is the matcher's defensible answer.

prompts.prompt: Everyone answers one question, then the answers get summed up into three themes for the board.

storyboard.name: Three Themes
storyboard.description: One open question, every answer read, three themes on the board to talk through.

steps.text: One question, everyone answers, and we will see the three big things this room is thinking.
What is one thing about this unit that still feels confusing?
Group the answers into exactly three themes. Give each theme a short plain heading and quote one answer under it, no names.
steps.heading: The three things this class is saying:

steps.text: Pick one theme and we will start there next time.

prompts.note: The summarize-brick case (storyboard probe, 2026-09-20): declined 3 of 3 while ai-process summarize had done it since the start. Discussion Starter is the matcher's defensible answer. The heading never names the AI.

prompts.prompt: Everyone draws a picture of me and then we vote on which one is the best.

storyboard.name: Portraits of the Teacher
storyboard.description: Everyone draws the teacher, the wall opens after a quick look, and the class votes for the best one.

steps.text: Ninety seconds to draw me. Be kind, or be funny, but be quick. Then the wall opens and you vote for the best one.
Draw a picture of your teacher.
steps.gallery: The portrait wall is open. Look closely, you vote next.

steps.text: Thank you, I think. The winner goes on the fridge.

prompts.note: The owner's own live try (2026-09-21): the matcher sent it to Creative Vote (a text box) once and Draw Gallery (no vote) twice; every recipe's answer box is typed, so a drawing idea with a vote is the step builder's (draw then vote). No acceptAlso: the vote is the heart, so Draw Gallery is not a defensible answer here.

prompts.prompt: A five-minute anonymous poll for my history class: what was the main cause of the American Revolution? The choices are taxation without representation, the Proclamation of 1763, the Boston Massacre, and Enlightenment ideas. Show the results, then we discuss.

params.question: What was the main cause of the American Revolution?

prompts.note: A reviewer's try (2026-09-23): the matcher answered with the Live Poll built-in ("Good news: this already exists") and Make it yours opened the default question about today's lesson, names Shown. The built-in is the live-poll recipe with its defaults, so the answer is the recipe with the teacher's question and all four of their choices; the route refits a recipe-born pick to its recipe as the net, and reads "anonymous" itself. No host: answer: the whole point is the content traveling.

prompts.prompt: Constitutional Convention: each student secretly gets a state, writes one clause their state needs, and the class votes clauses into a constitution that grows on the projector.

storyboard.name: Constitutional Convention
storyboard.description: Every delegate gets a state in secret, writes one clause, and the class votes.

steps.text: Welcome, delegates. Each of you represents one state. Nobody else knows which, so speak for your state, not yourself.
You represent {{thisStep.assigned}}. Write one clause your state needs in the constitution.
Which clause belongs in our constitution?
The convention is adjourned. Every state spoke, and the clause with the most votes leads our constitution.

prompts.note: An outside reviewer's try (2026-09-24): the storyboard reached for rank then assign, which lists every student's state on the projector, and the results step read {{vote.winner}}, a player id. The collect brick's items deal the states in private ({{thisStep.assigned}} on each student's screen, a blank on the projector), the vote brick appends the crown, and a vote's .winner in a step's words is rewritten to .winnerText.
